scope: Manual Khronos validation-layer chaining in front of the Vapor Vulkan wrapper and over the system libvulkan.so loader as a control (above-wrapper pass, top-level runs), plus a follow-up below-wrapper pass through the wrapper's built-in USE_VVL path (section below_wrapper_use_vvl) that puts the same layer between the wrapper and the llvmpipe driver. Offscreen native workload; no app/APK/Wine/Steam/game.

chaining_design: dlopen the Khronos layer and the driver/wrapper (or /system/lib64/libvulkan.so).
driver GIPA = vk_icdGetInstanceProcAddr if exported, else vkGetInstanceProcAddr.

instance: VkInstanceCreateInfo.pNext -> VkLayerInstanceCreateInfo{sType=47, function=VK_LAYER_LINK_INFO, u.pLayerInfo=&VkLayerInstanceLink{pfnNextGetInstanceProcAddr=driver GIPA, pfnNextGetPhysicalDeviceProcAddr=NULL}} -> VkLayerInstanceCreateInfo{sType=47, function=VK_LOADER_DATA_CALLBACK, u.pfnSetInstanceLoaderData=no-op}; create via the layer's vkCreateInstance obtained from its exported vkGetInstanceProcAddr.

device: VkDeviceCreateInfo.pNext -> VkLayerDeviceCreateInfo{sType=48, function=VK_LAYER_LINK_INFO, u.pLayerInfo=&VkLayerDeviceLink{pfnNextGetInstanceProcAddr=driver GIPA, pfnNextGetDeviceProcAddr=shim that resolves the driver's vkGetDeviceProcAddr via driver GIPA}} -> VkLayerDeviceCreateInfo{sType=48, function=VK_LOADER_DATA_CALLBACK, u.pfnSetDeviceLoaderData=no-op}.
No Vulkan loader is in the loop for the chained cases; validation messages are captured from the layer's default callback (stdout 'Validation Error: [ VUID-... ]' blocks and logcat tag VALIDATION).
VVL 1.4 keeps its own dispatch/handle maps (handle wrapping + _loader_data dispatch key); the loader-data callbacks are supplied for fidelity but the layer does not call them.
understood_limitations_of_layer_position: layer chained ABOVE the wrapper sees only application->wrapper API calls; the wrapper's own driver calls (BCn staging buffer/memory creation, compute dispatch, copies) happen below the layer
the wrapper's built-in USE_VVL route places the same layer BELOW the wrapper; it was executed in the below_wrapper_use_vvl section and exposed wrapper-internal defects D1 and D2

layer_interface_negotiation.exported_by_layer: vkNegotiateLoaderLayerInterfaceVersion (observed in the release library's dynamic symbols; fixture printed negotiate=1)
layer_interface_negotiation.interface_used_instead: layer's exported vkGetInstanceProcAddr / vkGetDeviceProcAddr via the loader-link chain, with positive/negative controls proving dispatch

summary.verdict: Above-wrapper manual chaining works and reports zero wrapper defects for the representative workloads (only the fixture's deliberate positive-control VUID); that pass validates the application-facing contract only. The follow-up below-wrapper USE_VVL pass put the same layer between the wrapper and the driver and found two wrapper-internal defects (D1: 14 wrapper-created driver objects leaked at every vkDestroyDevice; D2: HostSideDecompression leaves the source buffer host-mapped). limitations: The layer is manually chained ABOVE libvulkan_wrapper.so, so it validates the application->wrapper API contract only. The wrapper's own calls into the system loader/native driver (BCn staging VkBuffer/VkDeviceMemory, compute dispatch, copies) happen below the layer and are invisible here; a clean result is not evidence that wrapper-internal Vulkan usage is valid.

The layer position in this above-wrapper pass bounds its claim: wrapper-internal driver calls are invisible here. The below-wrapper USE_VVL route was executed in the follow-up section; it works on the API 36 userdebug emulator via android::GraphicsEnv layer paths and /data/local/tmp (not a portable or upstream-supported interface), and its limitations are listed in that section.

The manual loader-less chain relies on VVL's loader-data dispatch key; without a loader the wrapper's dispatchable objects all key to NULL, so the chain was exercised with exactly one instance and one device. Multiple instances/devices were not tested.

The fixture cannot install a VK_EXT_debug_utils messenger because the wrapper deliberately hides VK_EXT_debug_utils/VK_EXT_debug_report (wrapper_instance.c:158-159); the layer's default callback (stdout + logcat tag VALIDATION) was captured instead.
Runtime is llvmpipe software Vulkan inside the Android emulator with 4 KB pages (AVD VaporProbe36D, API 36, userdebug/dev-keys); no physical GPU, no Adreno/Mali driver, no game, APK, Wine or Steam.

The emulator was booted under heavy host co-tenancy (load average ~39-44); sys.boot_completed never became visible to the shell, so a documented fallback readiness check (activity service + package manager) was used, and the matrix ran about 3.5 minutes after the fallback became available.

Workloads are small offscreen images (16x16 BC1/BC3/RGBA8, up to 8 cycles, one two-region copy); they exercise the wrapper's BCn staging/compute/decode paths but are not a game workload and not a concurrency or performance test.

Both observed VUID-vkDestroyDevice-device-05137 occurrences are the fixture's deliberate positive-control leak; they are classified as fixture misuse, and the identical message on the system-loader chain confirms it is not wrapper-specific.
No validation-layer timing/performance claim is made; VVL adds overhead and the matrix was not timed for comparability.
The layer binary/build was used only as a loadable validation layer; its own correctness or its Android release provenance beyond the recorded release asset hash was not audited.

The fixture records that the layer exports vkNegotiateLoaderLayerInterfaceVersion but does not call it: the layer is driven through its exported vkGetInstanceProcAddr (the interface the loader negotiation would hand back), and the positive/negative controls prove that path dispatches. A negotiation-version assertion is therefore not part of this receipt.

comparison.conclusion: The manual VK_LAYER_LINK_INFO chain loaded and dispatched the official layer in both configurations; the deliberate positive controls reported the expected VUID through the wrapper chain and through the system-loader chain, and the no-layer negative control reported nothing. No VUID was reported for any representative wrapper workload (BC1 compute/image-view, BC3, host-CPU decode, two-region copy, caps, 8 cycles each), so nothing in this matrix is classifiable as a wrapper defect at the application-facing interface. This is a bounded negative result: the layer sits ABOVE the wrapper and cannot see the wrapper's internal driver calls (staging buffers, compute dispatch, copies).

layer_above_wrapper_sees_app_calls_only: wrapper_dispatch: WRAPPER_CmdCopyBufferToImage (wrapper_device.c:1555) allocates the BCn staging VkBuffer/VkDeviceMemory (wrapper_device.c:1013-1048, 1662-1678) and records the compute dispatch / staging->image copies (wrapper_device.c:1681-1760) directly against the system loader/driver

the manually chained layer in the top-level runs sits above the wrapper's exported vk_icdGetInstanceProcAddr interface, so those internal calls are below it and could not produce VUIDs there; the below_wrapper_use_vvl section covers them via the wrapper's USE_VVL path

executed in the below_wrapper_use_vvl section: layer found and enabled, negative control (USE_VVL=1 with no layer staged) failed with VK_ERROR_LAYER_NOT_PRESENT (-6), and the layer reported wrapper-internal defects D1/D2
loaderless_dispatch_key: VVL 1.4 locates its dispatch state from the first word (loader data / dispatch pointer) of dispatchable objects: layers/utils/dispatch_utils.h:26 GetDispatchKey().

Without a Vulkan loader, wrapper objects keep _loader_data == 0 (vk_object_base first member), so all dispatchable objects collapse to the same key. The manual chain therefore works for exactly one instance + one device (this fixture); multi-instance/multi-device chaining is untested.

conclusions: Manual loader-less chaining works: the official Khronos layer's vkCreateInstance / vkCreateDevice accepted the hand-built VK_LAYER_LINK_INFO (plus loader-data-callback) chains and dispatched every application call back down to the wrapper and to the system libvulkan.so loader control.

Layer liveness is proven, not assumed: with the chain in place a deliberately leaked VkBuffer + VkDeviceMemory produced VUID-vkDestroyDevice-device-05137 through BOTH the wrapper chain and the system-loader chain; the same fixture without the layer produced no message.

VUID count by class over the whole 13-run matrix: total validation messages = 2 (2 records, 1 VUID name); class fixture-misuse (deliberate positive control) = 2/2; wrapper defect = 0; chaining artefact = 0; emulator/driver issue = 0.

Wrapper-vs-control comparison: all six wrapper chained workloads that actually exercise the wrapper (BC1 compute view0, BC1 image-view, BC3, host-CPU decode, two-region copy, caps) and all three system-loader control workloads (BC1 native transfer, RGBA8, caps) exited 0 and reported zero validation messages; the fixture also passes without a layer, so the zero-message wrapper result is not a dispatch failure.

No wrapper defect was found at the application-facing interface under this workload, but the placement bounds the claim: the layer is above the wrapper and cannot see the wrapper's internal driver calls. The wrapper's own USE_VVL below-wrapper path was subsequently executed (below_wrapper_use_vvl) and found two wrapper-internal defects (D1 resource leak at vkDestroyDevice, D2 leaked source-buffer host mapping in the CPU decode path).

Wrapper-honest classification of the two observed messages: fixture misuse (positive control), not a wrapper defect, not a chaining artefact, not an emulator driver issue; the identical message on the system control chain confirms it is independent of the wrapper.

summary.verdict: The wrapper's USE_VVL path placed the official validation layer between the wrapper and the llvmpipe driver, and the layer immediately exposed two wrapper-internal defects that the above-wrapper pass could not see: D1 (14 wrapper-created driver objects never destroyed before driver vkDestroyDevice, every run) and D2 (the host-CPU decode path leaves the app's source buffer host-mapped, VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00678). All workloads still passed their pixel/readback checks.

comparison.above_vs_below: The above-wrapper matrix (top-level receipt) found 0 wrapper defects because it only sees the application-facing contract. The below-wrapper layer finds 2 wrapper-internal defects: D1 (14 driver objects left alive at every vkDestroyDevice, including the caps run) and D2 (source buffer host mapping leaked by the USE_CPU_BCN decode path).
comparison.conclusion: The below-wrapper route works end-to-end and turned the previously unvalidated gap into two concrete wrapper-source findings. Every workload still produced correct pixels/readbacks (RESULT ok), so the defects are teardown/mapping-lifetime issues rather than functional BCn decode failures.

conclusions: The documented below-wrapper route works: the wrapper's USE_VVL path found the staged layer via the GraphicsEnv layer-path hook, enabled VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation in the instance create info it passes to /system/lib64/libvulkan.so, and the layer validated the wrapper's internal driver calls. The negative control (USE_VVL=1 with no layer staged) failed instance creation with VK_ERROR_LAYER_NOT_PRESENT (-6), proving the wrapper really requests the layer.

All below-wrapper workloads (BC1 compute view0/image-view, BC3, host-CPU decode, two-region copy, caps) exited 0 with correct pixel/readback verification; the wrapper's BCn decode output remains functionally correct in this build.
These defects are invisible to the above-wrapper layer position and were missed by the earlier app-facing pass; this demonstrates why the below-wrapper route was needed.
limitations: Below-wrapper validation was only possible through the wrapper's own USE_VVL hook; it relies on dlopening android::GraphicsEnv and rewriting its layer path list to include /data/local/tmp (graphics_env_hooks.cpp:12,15-77). This worked on the API 36 userdebug emulator; it is not a device-independent or upstream-supported interface.

The layer is only loaded because the wrapper requests VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation in the instance create info it passes down; the negative control confirms that without a discoverable layer the wrapper refuses instance creation instead of running unvalidated.

The VVL log_file setting the wrapper passes points at /sdcard/Documents/Wrapper/, which the shell-domain native probe cannot open; VVL falls back to stdout. Those VALIDATION-SETTINGS warnings are environment-specific, not a wrapper defect.

One instance and one device per process; D1 objects are counted at driver vkDestroyDevice. A validation-enabled real app would also count any objects it leaks, so counts are only compared between builds of this same fixture.

D1's impact is bounded by the driver: llvmpipe's DestroyDevice frees leaked objects at device teardown, so this is an out-of-contract teardown/VUID, not a sustained process leak. A driver that asserts on live child objects at DestroyDevice could behave differently.
D2 is only reachable with the USE_CPU_BCN fallback (host decoding); the default compute/image-view decode paths do not map the source buffer.

Runtime is llvmpipe software Vulkan in the Android emulator (4 KB pages, API 36 userdebug); no physical GPU, no game, no concurrency stress, no performance claim. The emulator used the documented services-fallback readiness check under host co-tenancy.

The patched build is a staged wrapper-build directory; its wrapper .so hash is recorded in this section's wrapper_build/provenance block and compared by the A/B table. Nothing upstream was touched and no commit was made by this review.
The layer release provenance is the official Khronos release asset recorded in the provenance block; the layer's own correctness was not otherwise audited.

findings.title: Wrapper does not destroy its internal BCn compute resources before vkDestroyDevice
findings.kind: resource leak / spec violation at device teardown
findings.observed: Every below-wrapper run (including caps, which does no workload) reports 14 leaked driver objects at vkDestroyDevice: 3 VkPipeline, 3 VkPipelineLayout, 3 VkDescriptorSetLayout, 2 VkBuffer, 2 VkDeviceMemory and 1 VkCommandPool.

occurrences.note: The positive-control run also contains the same wrapper objects, so its leak count is 14 + the fixture's deliberate 1 VkBuffer + 1 VkDeviceMemory.

wrapper_source: wrapper_objects.h:77-84 InterceptorState (descriptorSetLayout, pipelineLayout, pipeline, constantsBuffer, constantsBufferMemory); wrapper_objects.h:106-111 wrapper_device.computePool + s3tc/bc6/bc7 states
wrapper_device.c:356-380 creates the three InterceptorState objects (s3tc, bc6, bc7) during device creation; wrapper_device.c:402 creates device->computePool
wrapper_device.c:874-1008 (InterceptorState_Init) creates the descriptor set layout (961), pipeline layout (977) and compute pipeline (1007); the shader module is destroyed (1008)
wrapper_device.c:839 declares CreateConstantsUniformBuffer; it is called for bc7 at 903 and bc6 at 928 and creates state->constantsBuffer + constantsBufferMemory (901-949)

wrapper_device.c:54 declares InterceptorState_Cleanup but it has no definition and no call site (grep over the pinned source); WRAPPER_DestroyDevice (wrapper_device.c:605-651) destroys command buffers, tracked device memory, images, buffers, command pools and queues, then calls the driver DestroyDevice at 644-647 without destroying the BCn compute resources or device->computePool
findings.impact: VUID violation / late-free at device destroy. The llvmpipe driver frees the objects inside its DestroyDevice, so this is not a sustained process leak or memory-safety issue, but it is a real out-of-contract teardown and would be reported by any validation-enabled run; repeated device create/destroy cycles inherit the same violation.
findings.fix: Call an implemented InterceptorState_Cleanup for s3tc/bc6/bc7 (DestroyPipeline, DestroyPipelineLayout, DestroyDescriptorSetLayout, DestroyBuffer + FreeMemory for the constants buffer) and vkDestroyCommandPool(device->computePool) before the driver DestroyDevice call in WRAPPER_DestroyDevice.
findings.classification: wrapper defect (below-wrapper layer, not visible from above)

findings.title: HostSideDecompression leaves the source buffer memory host-mapped
findings.kind: persistent host mapping / app-visible valid-usage violation
findings.observed: The host-CPU decode run (USE_CPU_BCN=all) reports 3 x VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00678 ('memory has already been mapped') on VkDeviceMemory 0x150000000015, one per cycle after the first, while the app's own map/unmap pairs are balanced.
wrapper_source: wrapper_device.c:1170-1190 HostSideDecompression maps srcBuffer->memory with MapMemory2KHR and never unmaps it

wrapper_device.c:1229 unmaps only the destination staging memory; the source unmap is commented out at wrapper_device.c:1231-1232 with the TODO 'this breaks some applications that maps the srcBuffer, e.g. 32bit emulated placeAddr'
the next cycle's application vkMapMemory on the same source buffer therefore traps below the wrapper as 'already mapped' (the wrapper's leaked mapping is what makes the app call invalid)
findings.impact: Real wrapper defect in the USE_CPU_BCN fallback: the wrapper permanently holds a host mapping of the application's source buffer, so any app that maps that buffer itself (the normal way to fill a staging buffer) hits VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00678 and may be broken on drivers that reject the double map. Only reachable with the CPU decode fallback; the default compute/image-view decode paths are unaffected.
findings.fix: Unmap srcBuffer->memory in HostSideDecompression (ideally on all paths, including failures) instead of leaving the mapping open.

below_layer_loaded_by_wrapper.meaning: The wrapper's set_layer_paths() hook rewrote GraphicsEnv layer paths to include /data/local/tmp, the wrapper enumerated VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation from the system loader and enabled it in the loader instance create info, so the layer runs below the wrapper.

negative_control.meaning: With USE_VVL=1 but no layer discoverable, the wrapper itself refuses instance creation with VK_ERROR_LAYER_NOT_PRESENT (-6): the wrapper really asks the system loader for VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation instead of silently running unvalidated.

positive_control.meaning: The deliberate app-level leak is always attributable to the fixture; in the unpatched build it appeared on top of 14 wrapper-internal leaks (16 total), in the patched build it should be the only leak (2 objects) and thereby keep the below-layer liveness proof even when D1 is fixed.

wrapper_internal_objects_visible.meaning: These are wrapper-internal BCn compute objects created at wrapper device init, not application handles: only a layer below the wrapper can report them, which proves the layer is between the wrapper and the driver.

expected_fix_liveness.meaning: With D1 fixed, the positive control must still produce exactly 2 leaked objects (fixture-owned VkBuffer + VkDeviceMemory) through the below-wrapper layer, which keeps the liveness proof independent of the wrapper leak.

findings.title: Wrapper does not destroy its internal BCn compute resources before vkDestroyDevice
findings.kind: resource leak / spec violation at device teardown
findings.observed: Every below-wrapper run (including caps, which does no workload) reports 14 leaked driver objects at vkDestroyDevice: 3 VkPipeline, 3 VkPipelineLayout, 3 VkDescriptorSetLayout, 2 VkBuffer, 2 VkDeviceMemory and 1 VkCommandPool.
findings.status: partially fixed (2 of 14 leaked objects remain; residual intentionally left to the driver)

occurrences.note: The positive-control run also contains the same wrapper objects, so its leak count is 14 + the fixture's deliberate 1 VkBuffer + 1 VkDeviceMemory.

wrapper_source: wrapper_objects.h:77-84 InterceptorState (descriptorSetLayout, pipelineLayout, pipeline, constantsBuffer, constantsBufferMemory); wrapper_objects.h:106-111 wrapper_device.computePool + s3tc/bc6/bc7 states
wrapper_device.c:356-380 creates the three InterceptorState objects (s3tc, bc6, bc7) during device creation; wrapper_device.c:402 creates device->computePool
wrapper_device.c:874-1008 (InterceptorState_Init) creates the descriptor set layout (961), pipeline layout (977) and compute pipeline (1007); the shader module is destroyed (1008)
wrapper_device.c:839 declares CreateConstantsUniformBuffer; it is called for bc7 at 903 and bc6 at 928 and creates state->constantsBuffer + constantsBufferMemory (901-949)

wrapper_device.c:54 declares InterceptorState_Cleanup but it has no definition and no call site (grep over the pinned source); WRAPPER_DestroyDevice (wrapper_device.c:605-651) destroys command buffers, tracked device memory, images, buffers, command pools and queues, then calls the driver DestroyDevice at 644-647 without destroying the BCn compute resources or device->computePool
findings.impact: VUID violation / late-free at device destroy. The llvmpipe driver frees the objects inside its DestroyDevice, so this is not a sustained process leak or memory-safety issue, but it is a real out-of-contract teardown and would be reported by any validation-enabled run; repeated device create/destroy cycles inherit the same violation.
findings.fix: Call an implemented InterceptorState_Cleanup for s3tc/bc6/bc7 (DestroyPipeline, DestroyPipelineLayout, DestroyDescriptorSetLayout, DestroyBuffer + FreeMemory for the constants buffer) and vkDestroyCommandPool(device->computePool) before the driver DestroyDevice call in WRAPPER_DestroyDevice.

remaining_objects: VkDeviceMemory x2 (the two BCn constants-buffer allocations)
residual.reason: The device-teardown patch frees 12 of the 14 wrapper-internal objects. The two constants VkDeviceMemory allocations are deliberately left to the driver: all wait-idle/unmap/wrapper-free variants crash gfxstream 10-15/40 runs, versus 0/40 for the 12/14 variant.
residual.status_note: Recorded as 'D1 partially fixed' (intentional residual), not as a failure.

findings.title: HostSideDecompression leaves the source buffer memory host-mapped
findings.kind: persistent host mapping / app-visible valid-usage violation
findings.observed: The host-CPU decode run (USE_CPU_BCN=all) reports 3 x VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00678 ('memory has already been mapped') on VkDeviceMemory 0x150000000015, one per cycle after the first, while the app's own map/unmap pairs are balanced.
wrapper_source: wrapper_device.c:1170-1190 HostSideDecompression maps srcBuffer->memory with MapMemory2KHR and never unmaps it

wrapper_device.c:1229 unmaps only the destination staging memory; the source unmap is commented out at wrapper_device.c:1231-1232 with the TODO 'this breaks some applications that maps the srcBuffer, e.g. 32bit emulated placeAddr'
the next cycle's application vkMapMemory on the same source buffer therefore traps below the wrapper as 'already mapped' (the wrapper's leaked mapping is what makes the app call invalid)
findings.impact: Real wrapper defect in the USE_CPU_BCN fallback: the wrapper permanently holds a host mapping of the application's source buffer, so any app that maps that buffer itself (the normal way to fill a staging buffer) hits VUID-vkMapMemory-memory-00678 and may be broken on drivers that reject the double map. Only reachable with the CPU decode fallback; the default compute/image-view decode paths are unaffected.
findings.fix: Unmap srcBuffer->memory in HostSideDecompression (ideally on all paths, including failures) instead of leaving the mapping open.
findings.classification: expected fix verified (not reproduced in this build)
